clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive disorder of males caused by RS1 mutations affecting retinoschisin, a protein needed for retinal cell adhesion and layer cohesion
Typically presents in boyhood with reduced central acuity; a classic sign is a spoke-wheel or cartwheel pattern of foveal cystic change radiating from the centre
Optical coherence tomography is diagnostic, showing splitting (schisis) of the inner retinal layers, most characteristically in the fovea, and often in the peripheral retina
Peripheral retinoschisis, when present, predisposes to vitreous haemorrhage and to schisis-related retinal detachment
The electroretinogram characteristically shows a selective reduction of the b-wave with relative preservation of the a-wave, giving an electronegative configuration
Fundus autofluorescence and OCT often reveal the foveal changes even when the spoke-wheel appearance is subtle on ophthalmoscopy

Management is supportive with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors sometimes used for the cystic maculopathy, surveillance for and repair of retinal detachment or vitreous haemorrhage, and genetic counselling; gene therapy is under investigation
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked retinoschisis is caused by mutations in RS1, encoding retinoschisin, a secreted adhesion protein produced by photoreceptors and bipolar cells that maintains the structural integrity and cell-to-cell adhesion of the retinal layers. Deficiency leads to splitting within the inner retina, classically at the fovea and often in the periphery, disrupting synaptic transmission between photoreceptors and bipolar cells. The impaired bipolar signalling accounts for the selectively reduced b-wave and electronegative electroretinogram, while structural schisis explains the cystic maculopathy and the risk of haemorrhage and detachment.
additionalDifferentials: Cystoid macular oedema from other causes
Goldmann-Favre syndrome and enhanced S-cone syndrome
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment or degenerative senile retinoschisis
Other causes of an electronegative electroretinogram such as congenital stationary night blindness
additionalInvestigations: Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography demonstrating inner retinal foveal schisis in a spoke-wheel pattern
Full-field electroretinography showing a selectively reduced b-wave (electronegative pattern)
Fundus autofluorescence and wide-field imaging for peripheral schisis
B-scan ultrasonography when vitreous haemorrhage obscures the view
Molecular genetic testing for RS1 mutations
Assessment of female relatives as potential carriers
redFlags: Sudden visual loss from vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment requiring urgent assessment
New floaters, field loss or a curtain in the vision indicating possible detachment
Bilateral macular schisis with declining central acuity
Family history along an X-linked pattern prompting screening of relatives
reference.prognosis: Central acuity is often reduced from childhood and may decline slowly with age; visual prognosis worsens if peripheral schisis leads to vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment, which can cause severe loss if untreated.
pitfalls: Mistaking foveal schisis for cystoid macular oedema and treating inappropriately
Failing to examine the peripheral retina for schisis and detachment risk
Attributing the electronegative electroretinogram to another disorder without OCT confirmation of schisis
Overlooking the X-linked inheritance and neglecting carrier and relative counselling
